source_note: ESSLCE Mathematics for Natural Science, Hamle 2015 E.C. (July 2023), booklet 340. Every answer re-checked. Q50 and Q65 are left out: no printed option is correct.

items.text: Given A = {x ∈ ℕ : x < 3} and B is the set of all possible factors of 13. Then, which one of the following is equal to B×A?
items.why:
1) A = {x ∈ ℕ : x < 3} = {1, 2}.
2) The positive factors of 13 are 1 and 13, so B = {1, 13}.
3) B×A = {(b, a) : b ∈ B, a ∈ A}: the first entry comes from B, the second from A.
4) B×A = {(1, 1), (1, 2), (13, 1), (13, 2)}. It has 2 × 2 = 4 pairs.
5) So the answer is A. (B is A×B: the order is reversed. C and D are missing pairs.)
items.review: Book says 'no answer' because it counts negative factors (B = {−13, −1, 1, 13}). Using the usual school meaning (positive factors), option A is exactly B×A.

items.text: Which of the following statements is true about f(x) = x² − 6x + 10?
opts: The line x = 1 is the axis of symmetry of graph of f.
f(x) ≥ 2 for all x in the domain of f.
The vertex of the graph of f is (3, 1).
The graph of f opens downward.
items.why:
1) Here a = 1, b = −6, c = 10.
2) Axis of symmetry: x = −b/(2a) = 6/2 = 3, not x = 1.
3) Vertex y-value: f(3) = 9 − 18 + 10 = 1. So the vertex is (3, 1).
4) a = 1 > 0, so the graph opens upward and the least value is 1, so f(x) ≥ 2 is false (f(3) = 1).
5) So the answer is C. (B is tempting, but the minimum is 1, not 2.)

items.text: What is the area of a regular hexagon inscribed in a circle of radius 6 cm?
items.why:
1) A regular hexagon in a circle splits into 6 equilateral triangles with side = radius = 6 cm.
2) Area of one equilateral triangle = (√3/4) × 6² = (√3/4) × 36 = 9√3 cm².
3) Hexagon area = 6 × 9√3 = 54√3 cm².
4) So the answer is A. (C, 36√3, uses 4 triangles instead of 6.)

items.text: Which of the following defines a prime number?
opts: It is a number whose only factor is 1.
It is a number that has more than two positive factors.
It is a number whose only factor is itself.
It is a number that has only two positive factor.
items.why:
1) A prime number is a natural number with exactly two positive factors: 1 and itself.
2) Example: 7 has factors 1 and 7 only.
3) B describes a composite number (e.g. 6 has 1, 2, 3, 6).
4) A and C leave out one of the two factors (every number > 1 has both 1 and itself).
5) So the answer is D.

items.text: Which one of the following rational numbers is written in its standard form?
items.why:
1) Standard form is a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10 and n an integer.
2) A: a = 0.888… < 1, not allowed.
3) B: a = 10.1 ≥ 10, not allowed.
4) D: a = 0.09 < 1, not allowed.
5) C: a = 5 and 1 ≤ 5 < 10, so 5 × 10⁵ is in standard form.
6) So the answer is C.

items.text: What is the value of x in the equation √(125ˣ · 5²ˣ⁻¹) = 25³ˣ⁺¹?
items.why:
1) Write everything as powers of 5: 125ˣ = (5³)ˣ = 5³ˣ and 25³ˣ⁺¹ = (5²)³ˣ⁺¹ = 5⁶ˣ⁺².
2) Inside the root: 5³ˣ · 5²ˣ⁻¹ = 5⁵ˣ⁻¹.
3) Square root halves the exponent: √(5⁵ˣ⁻¹) = 5^((5x−1)/2).
4) Equal bases, so equal exponents: (5x − 1)/2 = 6x + 2.
5) Multiply by 2: 5x − 1 = 12x + 4, so −7x = 5 and x = −5/7.
6) So the answer is A. (C, 5/7, comes from a sign slip when moving terms.)

items.text: The solution set of the equation 3|2x − 4| = 6 − 2|1 − 5x| is
items.why:
1) The left side 3|2x − 4| ≥ 0, so the right side must be ≥ 0: 6 − 2|1 − 5x| ≥ 0.
2) That gives |1 − 5x| ≤ 3, so −3 ≤ 1 − 5x ≤ 3, i.e. −2/5 ≤ x ≤ 4/5.
3) Also 2|1 − 5x| = 6 − 3|2x − 4| ≥ 0, so |2x − 4| ≤ 2, i.e. 1 ≤ x ≤ 3.
4) No x is in both [−2/5, 4/5] and [1, 3], so there is no solution.
5) Check a listed value: x = 1/2 gives left 3|−3| = 9, right 6 − 2|−1.5| = 3. Not equal.
6) So the answer is D, the empty set.

items.text: A regular pyramid has a hexagonal base whose side length is 12 cm. What is the lateral surface area of the pyramid in square centimeters if the length of each lateral edge is 10 cm?
items.why:
1) Each lateral face is an isosceles triangle with base 12 cm and equal sides (lateral edges) 10 cm.
2) Its height (the slant height) goes to the middle of the base: half the base is 6 cm.
3) Slant height = √(10² − 6²) = √(100 − 36) = √64 = 8 cm.
4) Area of one face = ½ × 12 × 8 = 48 cm².
5) Six faces: 6 × 48 = 288 cm².
6) So the answer is D. (B, 360, wrongly uses the lateral edge 10 cm as the triangle's height.)
items.review: Book key is B (360): it uses the lateral edge (10 cm) as the slant height in ½·n·s·ℓ. The slant height is √(10² − 6²) = 8 cm, giving 288 cm² = D.

items.text: The object shown in the figure below is made of wood. Its top cover is solid hemisphere and its bottom is a cylinder of base diameter 6 cm and height of 12 cm. From the bottom of the cylindrical part a right circular cone of height 8 cm is cut off. Thus, what is the volume of the solid in cubic centimeters?
items.figure: A solid made of a hemisphere sitting on top of a vertical cylinder of the same width; inside the cylinder a dashed cone stands on the bottom circular base with its apex pointing up (the hollow cut out from the bottom). No numbers on the figure; data (diameter 6 cm, cylinder height 12 cm, cone height 8 cm) are in the text.
items.why:
1) Radius r = 6/2 = 3 cm for the hemisphere, cylinder and cone.
2) Hemisphere: (2/3)πr³ = (2/3)π(27) = 18π.
3) Cylinder: πr²h = π(9)(12) = 108π.
4) Before the cut: 18π + 108π = 126π.
5) Cone removed: (1/3)πr²h = (1/3)π(9)(8) = 24π.
6) Remaining volume: 126π − 24π = 102π cm³.
7) So the answer is B. (C, 126π, forgets to remove the cone.)

items.text: The domain of the function f(x) = 2x^(2/3) is:
items.why:
1) x^(2/3) = (∛x)².
2) The cube root ∛x exists for every real x, including negatives (∛(−8) = −2).
3) Squaring is always possible, so f is defined for all real x.
4) So the domain is ℝ and the answer is D.
5) (A, [0, ∞), would be right for a square root, e.g. x^(1/2), but the root here is a cube root.)

items.text: The slope of a line that makes an angle of 135° with the positive x-axis is equal to:
items.why:
1) Slope m = tan θ, where θ is the angle with the positive x-axis.
2) m = tan 135°.
3) 135° is in quadrant II, where tan is negative: tan 135° = −tan(180° − 135°) = −tan 45° = −1.
4) So the answer is A. (D, 1, forgets the negative sign in quadrant II.)

items.text: If tan 31° = 0.81, then what is the value of tan 509°
items.why:
1) Remove a full turn: 509° − 360° = 149°, so tan 509° = tan 149°.
2) 149° is in quadrant II: tan 149° = −tan(180° − 149°) = −tan 31°.
3) So tan 509° = −0.81.
4) So the answer is A. (D, 0.81, ignores that tan is negative in quadrant II.)

items.text: If sin θ = −3/5 and θ is 4th quadrant angle, then what is the value of sec θ?
items.why:
1) cos²θ = 1 − sin²θ = 1 − 9/25 = 16/25, so cos θ = ±4/5.
2) In quadrant IV, cos is positive: cos θ = 4/5.
3) sec θ = 1/cos θ = 5/4.
4) So the answer is A. (C, −5/4, takes the wrong sign; B/D use 1/sin θ, which is csc θ.)

items.text: Suppose ABCD is a parallelogram with P a mid-point of AB (segment) and Q a mid-point of CD (segment). Then which of the following is NOT necessarily true?
items.why:
1) AP = ½AB and QC = ½CD. Since AB = CD and AB ∥ CD, AP = QC and AP ∥ QC.
2) So APCQ is a parallelogram, which makes AQ ≡ PC (A is true).
3) AD = CB, ∠D = ∠B, DQ = BP, so ΔADQ ≡ ΔCBP by SAS (B is true).
4) AP ∥ DC, while AD and PC are not parallel, so APCD is a trapezium (D is true).
5) A rhombus needs AP = PC; PC can be much longer than AP (e.g. a long, slanted parallelogram). So C is not necessarily true.
6) So the answer is C.

items.text: The solution set of the equation 5log₉x − 2log₉(x²) − log₄8 = −1 is
items.why:
1) We need x > 0.
2) log₄8 = log₄(4^(3/2)) = 3/2.
3) log₉(x²) = 2log₉x. Let y = log₉x.
4) 5y − 2(2y) − 3/2 = −1, so y − 3/2 = −1, so y = 1/2.
5) log₉x = 1/2 means x = 9^(1/2) = 3.
6) So the answer is A. (D, 9, comes from taking y = 1.)

items.text: What is the value of x that satisfies the equation 5(125/8)^((1/3)x² − (2/3)x) = 2?
items.why:
1) Divide by 5: (125/8)^((1/3)x² − (2/3)x) = 2/5.
2) 125/8 = (5/2)³, so the left side is (5/2)^(x² − 2x).
3) 2/5 = (5/2)⁻¹.
4) Equal bases: x² − 2x = −1, so x² − 2x + 1 = 0.
5) (x − 1)² = 0, so x = 1.
6) So the answer is B. (Check: x = 1 gives exponent −1/3, and (125/8)^(−1/3) = 2/5, so 5 × 2/5 = 2.)

items.text: The solution set of the inequality (2x − 3)(x + 5) ≤ 0 is
items.why:
1) Zeros: 2x − 3 = 0 gives x = 3/2; x + 5 = 0 gives x = −5.
2) The product is an upward parabola, so it is ≤ 0 between the zeros.
3) Include the zeros because of '≤'.
4) Solution: [−5, 3/2].
5) So the answer is C. (B leaves out the endpoints; A is where the product is ≥ 0.)

items.text: The histogram below shows the recorded temperature (in °C) of certain town in Ethiopia for the first 15 days of March 2023. Then which one of the following statements is true about the data represented by the histogram?
items.figure: Bar histogram. Vertical axis 'Frequency' with labels 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 (grid lines continue above). Horizontal axis 'Temperature' with bars at 15, 17, 19, 21, 22, 24 (last label printed as '2'). Bar heights: 15 → 1, 17 → 2, 19 → 2, 21 → 1, 22 → 5 (tallest), 24 → 3.
opts: The mode of the data is 22 °C.
The temperature was 24 °C for two days.
For 45% of the days, the temperature was more than 19 °C.
items.why:
1) Read the bars: 15 °C → 1, 17 °C → 2, 19 °C → 2, 21 °C → 1, 22 °C → 5, 24 °C → 3.
2) The tallest bar is 22 °C (frequency 5), so the mode is 22 °C (A true, D false).
3) 24 °C has frequency 3, not 2 (B false).
4) More than 19 °C: 1 + 5 + 3 = 9 days out of 1+2+2+1+5+3 = 14, about 64%, not 45% (C false).
5) So the answer is A.
items.review: Printed figure is cut off (axis labels stop at 4, last x-label shows '2'); heights taken from the book's solution table (1, 2, 2, 1, 5, 3), which sum to 14, not the 15 days in the stem. Answer A is unaffected.

items.text: A 20 m high building casts a shadow of 4 m, at the same time a 35 m tree casts a shadow of x m. What is the value of x?
items.why:
1) At the same time the sun's rays make the same angle, so height and shadow are in the same ratio.
2) shadow/height: 4/20 = x/35.
3) x = 35 × 4/20 = 35 × 0.2 = 7 m.
4) So the answer is D. (A, 11 m, adds the 15 m height difference wrongly instead of using a ratio.)

items.text: A car started moving 9 km to the East then moved 4 km to the North and then 12 km towards West to reach its destination. How far the care travelled from its starting point?
items.why:
1) 'How far from its starting point' asks for the straight-line distance (displacement) from start to end.
2) East–west: 9 km East then 12 km West gives 3 km West.
3) North–south: 4 km North.
4) Straight-line distance = √(3² + 4²) = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5 km.
5) So the answer is C. (B, 25 km, is the total path length 9 + 4 + 12, not the distance from the start.)
items.review: Book key is B (25 km, total path length). The question asks how far the car is 'from its starting point', which is the displacement magnitude 5 km (C); the 3-4-5 numbers confirm this intent. Teacher may want to confirm.

items.text: When the polynomial p(x) = 3x⁶ + 5x⁴ − 7x³ + 2kx² + 3 is divided by x + 1, the remainder is 4. What is the value of k?
items.why:
1) Remainder theorem: dividing by x + 1 = x − (−1) leaves remainder p(−1).
2) p(−1) = 3(1) + 5(1) − 7(−1) + 2k(1) + 3 = 3 + 5 + 7 + 2k + 3 = 18 + 2k.
3) 18 + 2k = 4, so 2k = −14 and k = −7.
4) So the answer is A. (B, −5, comes from taking −7(−1)³ as −7.)

items.text: The equation of a parabola with vertex V(2, −1) and focus F(−1, −1) is
items.why:
1) Vertex and focus share y = −1, so the axis is horizontal: form (y − k)² = 4p(x − h).
2) The focus is to the left of the vertex (−1 < 2), so the parabola opens left.
3) Distance vertex to focus: |2 − (−1)| = 3, so 4p = −12 (negative because it opens left).
4) Equation: (y + 1)² = −12(x − 2).
5) So the answer is A. (D opens to the right, away from the focus.)

items.text: What is the equation of the hyperbola with foci F₁ = (−2, 1), F₂ = (8, 1) and the length of the conjugate axis is 8 units?
items.why:
1) Centre = midpoint of the foci = ((−2 + 8)/2, (1 + 1)/2) = (3, 1).
2) 2c = 8 − (−2) = 10, so c = 5 and c² = 25.
3) Conjugate axis 2b = 8, so b = 4 and b² = 16.
4) a² = c² − b² = 25 − 16 = 9.
5) Foci lie on y = 1 (horizontal), so: (x − 3)²/9 − (y − 1)²/16 = 1.
6) Option D has a² = 9 and b² = 16 but prints the centre as (5, 1) instead of (3, 1); it is the closest option.
7) (A swaps a² and b² and uses c² for b²; C uses c² as a².)
items.review: No option is exactly correct; the book also says 'no answer'. Correct equation is (x − 3)²/9 − (y − 1)²/16 = 1. Option D matches except for (x − 5) instead of (x − 3), probably a misprint. Answer set to D; consider correcting option D's text before use.

items.text: If the truth value of p is T, then which of the following compound propositions has a truth value T for any proposition q?
items.why:
1) p is T, so ¬p is F.
2) A: ¬p ∧ q = F ∧ q = F, and F ⇒ q is always T. So A is T for any q.
3) B: p ∨ ¬q = T, so ¬p ⇔ T = F ⇔ T = F.
4) C: (p ⇒ q) ∧ F = F.
5) D: p ∧ ¬p = F, so F ∧ q = F.
6) So the answer is A.

items.text: Which of the following functions is one to one?
opts: f = {(x, y): y is the mother of x}
items.why:
1) One-to-one means different inputs always give different outputs.
2) A: for x > 0, |x| = x, so f(x) = x − 1, a line with slope 1. Different x give different values: one-to-one.
3) B: f(1) = 5 and f(6) = 5. Two inputs, same output: not one-to-one.
4) C: siblings have the same mother: not one-to-one.
5) D: f(−1) = f(1) = 0: not one-to-one.
6) So the answer is A. (On all of ℝ, |x| − 1 would fail; the domain (0, ∞) makes it work.)

items.text: If (x² + 14)/((x + 2)(x − 1)²) = A/(x + 2) + B/(x − 1) + C/(x − 1)², then what are the values of A, B and C respectively?
items.why:
1) Multiply both sides by (x + 2)(x − 1)²: x² + 14 = A(x − 1)² + B(x − 1)(x + 2) + C(x + 2).
2) Put x = 1: 1 + 14 = 3C, so C = 5.
3) Put x = −2: 4 + 14 = 9A, so A = 2.
4) Compare x² coefficients: 1 = A + B, so B = 1 − 2 = −1.
5) So A, B, C = 2, −1, 5: answer C.
6) (D has B = −2: check x = 0: 14 = A − 2B + 2C = 2 + 2 + 10 = 14 with B = −1, but D gives 2 + 4 − 10 = −4.)

items.text: Which of the following is true about the intercept and symmetry of the graph of f(x) = (x³ − 3x)/(x² − 6)?
opts: The graph is symmetrical with respect to the y-axis.
The graph is symmetrical with respect to the origin.
items.why:
1) y-intercept: f(0) = (0 − 0)/(0 − 6) = 0, so A is false.
2) Test symmetry: f(−x) = ((−x)³ − 3(−x))/((−x)² − 6) = (−x³ + 3x)/(x² − 6).
3) That equals −(x³ − 3x)/(x² − 6) = −f(x), so f is odd.
4) An odd function is symmetric about the origin, so C is true and B (y-axis, even functions) is false.
5) x-intercepts: x³ − 3x = 0 → x(x² − 3) = 0 → x = 0, ±√3.
6) D is tempting, but ±√6 make the DENOMINATOR zero: they are vertical asymptotes, not intercepts.
7) So the answer is C.

items.text: Consider the lines ℓ₁: y = 2x + 3 and ℓ₂: y = 1 − 3x. Then the angle between ℓ₁ and ℓ₂ is
items.why:
1) Slopes: m₁ = 2 and m₂ = −3.
2) tan θ = |(m₂ − m₁)/(1 + m₁m₂)|.
3) m₂ − m₁ = −3 − 2 = −5; 1 + m₁m₂ = 1 + 2(−3) = −5.
4) tan θ = |−5/−5| = 1, so θ = π/4.
5) D (π/2) would need m₁m₂ = −1, but here m₁m₂ = −6. A (3π/2) is bigger than any angle between two lines.
6) So the answer is B.

items.text: Let u = (−1, 6) and v = (2, 4) be position vectors. Then the value of 4u − 3v is
Which of the following is true about the graph of y = 3sin(4x)?
opts: The graph lies below x-axis on (π/4, π/2).
The graph completes one cycle on the interval [0, π].
The graph rises up on [0, π/4].
The graph completes one cycle on the interval [0, π/4].
items.why:
1) Period = 2π/4 = π/2, so one full cycle is [0, π/2].
2) For x in (π/4, π/2), 4x is in (π, 2π), where sine is negative.
3) So y = 3sin(4x) < 0 there: the graph is below the x-axis. A is true.
4) On [0, π] the graph makes 2 cycles, so B is false; [0, π/4] is only half a cycle, so D is false.
5) sin rises only for 4x in [0, π/2], i.e. x in [0, π/8]; after π/8 it falls. So C is false.
6) So the answer is A.

items.text: If a translation T takes a point (−1, 1) to point (3, 2), then the image of the circle x² + y² − 2x + 4y + 1 = 0 under T is
items.why:
1) Translation vector: (3, 2) − (−1, 1) = (4, 1).
2) Complete squares: (x² − 2x + 1) + (y² + 4y + 4) = −1 + 1 + 4 → (x − 1)² + (y + 2)² = 4.
3) Centre (1, −2), radius 2.
4) A translation moves the centre and keeps the radius: (1 + 4, −2 + 1) = (5, −1).
5) Image: (x − 5)² + (y + 1)² = 4.
6) A, B and C keep radius 2 but put the centre in the wrong place; always add (4, 1) to the centre (1, −2).
7) So the answer is D.
items.review: Part of the circle equation is covered by a watermark; the reading x² + y² − 2x + 4y + 1 = 0 is confirmed by the book's worked solution.

items.text: Let A be a square matrix of order n and let B be a matrix obtained by multiplying one row of A by 2 and C be a matrix found by adding one row of A to another row of A. If det(A) = 10, what are det(B) and det(C)?
items.why:
1) Multiplying one row by 2 multiplies the determinant by 2: det(B) = 2 × 10 = 20.
2) Adding a multiple of one row to another row does not change the determinant: det(C) = 10.
3) A (0) would be true only if two rows became equal; adding rows does not do that.
4) So the answer is B.

items.text: The solution set of the system {2x − y + 3z = 1; x + y + 3z = 5; x − y + z = −1} is
items.why:
1) Add equations 1 and 2: 3x + 6z = 6, so x = 2 − 2z.
2) Subtract equation 3 from equation 2: 2y + 2z = 6, so y = 3 − z.
3) Check in equation 1: 2(2 − 2z) − (3 − z) + 3z = 4 − 4z − 3 + z + 3z = 1. ✓ Always true, so infinitely many solutions.
4) Let z = k: (x, y, z) = (2 − 2k, 3 − k, k).
5) Test A with k = 0: (1, 0, −1) gives 2 − 0 − 3 = −1 ≠ 1, so A fails.
6) So the answer is D.

items.text: Let z₁, z₂ and z₃ be complex numbers. Then which one of the following is NOT necessarily true?
items.why:
1) Open the bracket in A: z₁ − (z₂ − z₃) = z₁ − z₂ + z₃.
2) The right side is z₁ − z₂ − z₃. These differ unless z₃ = 0. So A is not always true.
3) B: z₁ − z₂ − z₃ on both sides, always true.
4) C is associativity and D is commutativity of multiplication; both hold for complex numbers.
5) So the answer is A.

items.text: Which one of the following complex numbers corresponds to the point (−3, −1) in the Argand plane?
items.why:
1) The point (a, b) in the Argand plane is the number a + bi.
2) (−3, −1) → −3 + (−1)i = −3 − i.
3) D swaps the real and imaginary parts; B has the wrong sign on i.
4) So the answer is C.

items.text: A group of students, 5 from grade 10, 8 from grade 11 and 2 from grade 12 to be formed. If a student is chosen randomly from this group, what is the probability that the chosen student is either from grade 10 or from grade 12?
items.why:
1) Total students: 5 + 8 + 2 = 15.
2) Grade 10 or grade 12: 5 + 2 = 7 (the groups do not overlap).
3) P = 7/15.
4) A (5/15) counts only grade 10; you must add the 2 grade-12 students too.
5) So the answer is B.

items.text: If [[2, −1], [a, 4]] × [[1, b], [−1, 3]] = [[3, 1], [−1, 18]], then what are the values of a and b respectively?
items.why:
1) Multiply row by column: top-left 2(1) + (−1)(−1) = 3. ✓
2) Top-right: 2b + (−1)(3) = 2b − 3. Set equal to 1: b = 2.
3) Bottom-left: a(1) + 4(−1) = a − 4. Set equal to −1: a = 3.
4) Check bottom-right: ab + 4(3) = 6 + 12 = 18. ✓
5) D swaps the roles; the order asked is a then b.
6) So the answer is B.

1) The transpose turns each row into a column: A is 3×2, so Aᵀ is 2×3.
2) First column of A (1, 0, −3) becomes row 1 of Aᵀ.
3) Second column of A (−1, 2, 6) becomes row 2.
4) Aᵀ = [[1, 0, −3], [−1, 2, 6]].
5) D has the right rows in the wrong order; A and C are still 3×2.
6) So the answer is B.

items.text: In a certain month of a year, the temperature of a city was recorded and presented as follows. Which one of the following is the cumulative frequency of the fourth class?
items.figure: Table: Temperature (in °C) classes 10-14, 15-19, 20-24, 25-29, 30-34; Frequency (Number of days) 2, 9, 11, 5, 3.
items.why:
1) Cumulative frequency of a class = sum of frequencies up to and including it.
2) Running totals: 2, 2 + 9 = 11, 11 + 11 = 22, 22 + 5 = 27, 27 + 3 = 30.
3) Fourth class (25–29): 27.
4) B (22) is the third class's cumulative frequency; stop one class later.
5) So the answer is A.

items.text: On set of Natural numbers ℕ, which one of the following propositions has a truth value True?
items.why:
1) B: take x = y = 1. Then x − y = 0 = y − x. One example is enough for ∃∃, so B is true.
2) A: x = 1, y = 2 gives x ≠ y true but x > y false, so A is false.
3) C: xy < x needs y < 1, and no natural number is less than 1. False.
4) D: for x = 1, x − y = 5 needs y = −4, not natural. False.
5) So the answer is B.

items.text: The following is distribution of the weight of 40 students in a certain class. Then, for the data given above, what is the median weight in Kg?
items.figure: Table: Weight (in Kg) classes 40-48, 49-57, 58-66, 67-75, 76-84; Frequency f 8, 18, 7, 5, 2.
items.why:
1) n = 40, so the median is the 20th value.
2) Cumulative frequencies: 8, 26, 33, 38, 40. The 20th value is in 49–57.
3) Class boundaries: 48.5–57.5, so L = 48.5, width i = 9.
4) Cf before = 8, f = 18.
5) Median = L + ((n/2 − Cf)/f) × i = 48.5 + ((20 − 8)/18) × 9 = 48.5 + 6 = 54.5.
6) Using the class limit 49 instead of the boundary 48.5 gives 55 (option A).
7) So the answer is B.

items.text: A fair die is going to be rolled once and let events be given as; E₁ = an even number occurs; E₂ = a prime number occurs; E₃ = a multiple of 3 occurs; E₄ = a multiple of 5 occurs. Then, which one of the following pairs of events is mutually exclusive?
items.why:
1) List outcomes: E₁ = {2, 4, 6}, E₂ = {2, 3, 5}, E₃ = {3, 6}, E₄ = {5}.
2) Mutually exclusive means no common outcome.
3) E₃ ∩ E₄ = ∅, so they are mutually exclusive.
4) E₁ ∩ E₃ = {6}, E₂ ∩ E₄ = {5}, E₁ ∩ E₂ = {2}: all share an outcome.
5) So the answer is A.

items.text: Which of the following is true about zero(s) of a function f(x)?
opts: If f(a) = 0, then y = a is the y-intercept.
If f(a) = 0, then x − a is a factor of f(x).
If f(a) = 0, then a is not necessarily in the domain of f.
If f(a) = 0, then (x − a)² is a factor of f(x)
items.why:
1) f(a) = 0 means a is a zero: the graph meets the x-axis at (a, 0), not the y-axis. A is false.
2) Factor theorem (for polynomials): f(a) = 0 ⇔ (x − a) is a factor of f(x). So B is the intended answer.
3) C is false: f(a) can only be evaluated if a is in the domain.
4) D is false: (x − a)² is a factor only for a repeated zero, e.g. f(x) = x − 1 has zero 1 but (x − 1)² is not a factor.
5) So the answer is B (true when f is a polynomial).
items.review: Book marks this a 'Wrong Item': B holds only for polynomials (e.g. f(x) = 2ˣ − 1 has zero 0 but x is not a factor). Exam context is polynomials, so B is given as the intended answer; teacher may wish to add 'polynomial' to the stem.

items.text: What is the value of a number in the interval (0, 1) that satisfies the Mean Value Theorem for the function f(x) = 3x² − 5x + 1?
items.why:
1) f is a polynomial, so it is continuous on [0, 1] and differentiable on (0, 1).
2) f(0) = 1 and f(1) = 3 − 5 + 1 = −1.
3) Average slope: (f(1) − f(0))/(1 − 0) = (−1 − 1)/1 = −2.
4) f'(x) = 6x − 5. Set 6c − 5 = −2, so c = 3/6 = 1/2.
5) D (5/6) solves f'(c) = 0, which is Rolle's case, not this one; C (1) is not inside (0, 1).
6) So the answer is B.

items.text: Water is running into a conical tank which is pointed down at a constant rate of 6π cm³/sec. The cone has a height of 10 cm and base radius 5 cm. How fast is the water level rising when the water reaches 2 cm deep?
items.why:
1) Volume of a cone: V = (1/3)πr²h.
2) Similar triangles: r/h = 5/10, so r = h/2.
3) Substitute: V = (1/3)π(h/2)²h = (1/12)πh³.
4) Differentiate in t: dV/dt = (1/4)πh² · dh/dt.
5) So dh/dt = 4/(πh²) · dV/dt.
6) At h = 2: dh/dt = 4/(π·4) · 6π = 6 cm/sec.
7) So the answer is A. (C, 6/π, forgets that dV/dt already contains π.)
items.review: Paper prints 'canonical tank'; it means 'conical tank'.

items.text: Let f(x) = 1/√x and g(x) = 2 − (1/6)x³ be two functions. For what values of x do the graphs of f and g have tangent lines of the same slope?
items.why:
1) Same slope means f′(x) = g′(x).
2) f(x) = x^(−1/2), so f′(x) = −(1/2)x^(−3/2).
3) g′(x) = −(1/6)·3x² = −(1/2)x².
4) Set equal: x^(−3/2) = x², so x^(7/2) = 1.
5) For x > 0 this gives x = 1.
6) So the answer is A. (D, 4, gives f′(4) = −1/16 but g′(4) = −8: not equal.)

items.text: Which of the following describes the mechanical meaning of derivative?
items.why:
1) The 'mechanical' (physical) meaning is about motion and change.
2) The derivative of position with respect to time is velocity.
3) Velocity is the instantaneous rate of change of position.
4) So the answer is D. (B and C are the geometric meaning, not the mechanical one; A is the integral.)

items.text: Let f(x) = 5x³ + 2x − sin x + eˣ. What is the value of f′(0)?
items.why:
1) Differentiate term by term.
2) f′(x) = 15x² + 2 − cos x + eˣ.
3) At x = 0: f′(0) = 15(0) + 2 − cos 0 + e⁰.
4) = 0 + 2 − 1 + 1 = 2.
5) So the answer is B. (A, 1, forgets the derivative of eˣ is eˣ, which adds 1.)
items.review: Paper prints 'What is he value of f′(x)?'; the book's solution evaluates f′(0), which the numeric options require. Text corrected to f′(0); last term eˣ is partly hidden by a watermark (confirmed by the solution).

items.text: Let f and g be differentiable functions and h(x) = g(f(3x+1)). If f′(1) = f(1) = 2 and g′(2) = 1, then what is the value of h′(0)?
items.why:
1) Chain rule: h′(x) = g′(f(3x+1)) · f′(3x+1) · 3.
2) At x = 0: 3x + 1 = 1.
3) h′(0) = g′(f(1)) · f′(1) · 3.
4) f(1) = 2, so g′(f(1)) = g′(2) = 1.
5) h′(0) = 1 · 2 · 3 = 6.
6) So the answer is D. (B, 2, forgets the factor 3 from the inside 3x + 1.)

items.text: What is the coordinate of the mid-point of the line segment joining (−1, −3, 3) and (−1, 5, −7) in space?
items.why:
1) Midpoint = ((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2, (z₁+z₂)/2).
2) x: (−1 + (−1))/2 = −1.
3) y: (−3 + 5)/2 = 1.
4) z: (3 + (−7))/2 = −2.
5) So the answer is D. (C subtracts instead of adding the coordinates.)

items.text: Which of the following assertions is true applying the Principle of Mathematical Induction?
items.why:
1) Test small cases first, then prove the survivor.
2) A: n = 1 gives 1! = 1 ≥ 2, false.
3) C: n = 1 gives 3 = 1², false.
4) D: n = 2 gives 2 = 3 + 1 = 4, false.
5) B: base n = 0: 1 = 2¹ − 1. True.
6) Step: if 1 + … + 2ᵏ = 2ᵏ⁺¹ − 1, add 2ᵏ⁺¹: total 2·2ᵏ⁺¹ − 1 = 2ᵏ⁺² − 1.
7) So B holds for all n ≥ 0; the answer is B. (A looks true for n = 0 and large n, but fails at n = 1, 2, 3.)

items.text: Let F be the anti-derivative of f. Then which of the following is NOT true about F and f?
items.why:
1) F is an anti-derivative of f means F′ = f. So A is true.
2) Integrating a derivative gives back the function plus a constant: ∫f′(x)dx = f(x) + c. So C is true.
3) Integrating F does not give f; it gives a function whose derivative is F.
4) Check D: d/dx(f + c) = f′, which is not F in general. So D is false.
5) So the answer is D. (B is also slightly off: d/dx ∫F dx equals F(x) exactly, with no + c.)
items.review: Book key says 'B and D'. D is the clear intended answer; B is also technically false because of the '+ c'. Suggested fix: print B as d/dx ∫F(x)dx = F(x).

items.text: Which of the following is equal to ∫ 3 cos 3x dx?
items.why:
1) Let u = 3x, so du = 3 dx.
2) ∫3 cos 3x dx = ∫cos u du.
3) = sin u + c = sin 3x + c.
4) Check: d/dx(sin 3x) = 3 cos 3x. ✓
5) So the answer is A. (B is ∫cos 3x dx, which forgets the 3 in front.)

items.text: What is the area of the region bounded by the graph of f(x) = x² − 4 and x-axis in square units?
items.why:
1) x² − 4 = 0 at x = −2 and x = 2.
2) On [−2, 2] the graph is below the x-axis, so area = ∫ from −2 to 2 of (4 − x²) dx.
3) By symmetry: area = 2∫ from 0 to 2 of (4 − x²) dx.
4) = 2[4x − x³/3] from 0 to 2 = 2(8 − 8/3).
5) = 2 · 16/3 = 32/3.
6) So the answer is C. (D, 16/3, is only the half from 0 to 2.)

items.text: Let f be a continuous function on [0, 1] and let F be an anti-derivative of f with F(1) = −11 and F(0) = 11. Then ∫₀¹ f(x)dx is equal to
items.why:
1) Fundamental Theorem: ∫₀¹ f(x)dx = F(1) − F(0).
2) = −11 − 11.
3) = −22.
4) So the answer is B. (C, 22, subtracts in the wrong order: F(0) − F(1).)

items.text: Which of the following set of equations define the xz-plane?
opts: {(x, y, z) | x, y, z ∈ ℝ and y = 0}
{(x, y, z) | x, y, z ∈ ℝ and x = z = 0}
{(x, y, z) | x, y, z ∈ ℝ and z = 0}
{(x, y, z) | x, y, z ∈ ℝ and x = 0}
items.why:
1) The xz-plane contains the x-axis and the z-axis.
2) On it x and z are free, and the missing coordinate is y.
3) So the plane is y = 0.
4) The answer is A. (C, z = 0, is the xy-plane; B, x = z = 0, is the y-axis, a line.)

items.text: Let the sequence {aₙ} converges to 3 while {bₙ} converges to −1. Then the sequence {aₙ − bₙ} converges to
items.why:
1) The limit of a difference is the difference of the limits.
2) lim(aₙ − bₙ) = lim aₙ − lim bₙ.
3) = 3 − (−1) = 4.
4) So the answer is A. (B, 1, is 3 + (−1): it adds instead of subtracting.)

items.text: What is the value of lim (x→1) (x² − 1)/(x² + 1)?
items.why:
1) The denominator x² + 1 is never 0, so the function is continuous at 1.
2) Substitute x = 1 directly.
3) (1 − 1)/(1 + 1) = 0/2 = 0.
4) So the answer is C. (Do not cancel as if it were (x² − 1)/(x − 1); that would give 2, option D.)

items.text: Which of the following is the value of α so that the function given by f(x) = {αx + 1, x ≥ 1; x² − 4, x < 1} is continuous at 1?
items.why:
1) Continuity at 1 needs left limit = right limit = f(1).
2) Left limit: lim (x→1⁻) (x² − 4) = 1 − 4 = −3.
3) Right limit and f(1): α(1) + 1 = α + 1.
4) Set equal: α + 1 = −3, so α = −4.
5) So the answer is A. (B, 4, comes from a sign slip, taking the left limit as +3 and then mis-solving; the left limit is 1 − 4 = −3.)
items.review: The exponent in x² − 4 is smudged on the scan; read as x² (confirmed by the book's solution).

items.text: Which of the following functions has a graph that completes one full cycle on [−π/4, 11π/4]?
items.why:
1) Length of the interval: 11π/4 − (−π/4) = 12π/4 = 3π.
2) Period of a sin(kx + b) is 2π/k. We need 2π/k = 3π, so k = 2/3.
3) A: 2π/(4/3) = 3π/2. B: 2π/3. C: π. D: 2π/(2/3) = 3π.
4) Check D starts a cycle at x = −π/4: (2/3)(−π/4) + π/6 = −π/6 + π/6 = 0. ✓
5) So the answer is D. (A has period 3π/2, so it makes two cycles on this interval.)

items.text: Let f(x) = −(1/3)cos((3/2)x − π/3). Then what is the period and phase shift of the graph of f respectively?
items.why:
1) For a cos(kx + b): period = 2π/k, phase shift = −b/k.
2) Here k = 3/2 and b = −π/3.
3) Period = 2π ÷ (3/2) = 4π/3.
4) Phase shift = −(−π/3) ÷ (3/2) = (π/3)·(2/3) = 2π/9.
5) So the answer is B. (A uses 2π/3, which divides by 3 instead of by 3/2.)

items.text: What is the fifth term of the sequence {2ⁿ + 4n − 5} from n = 0 to ∞?
items.why:
1) The index starts at n = 0, so the terms are n = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.
2) The fifth term is at n = 4.
3) 2⁴ + 4(4) − 5 = 16 + 16 − 5 = 27.
4) So the answer is B. (D, 47, uses n = 5: 32 + 20 − 5.)

items.text: Which one of the following numbers is the upper bound of the sequence {(2n+1)/(n+1)} from n = 1 to ∞?
items.why:
1) Rewrite: (2n+1)/(n+1) = 2 − 1/(n+1).
2) Since 1/(n+1) > 0, every term is less than 2.
3) Terms: 3/2, 5/3, 7/4, … rising toward 2.
4) Any number ≥ 2 is an upper bound; among the options only 4 works.
5) So the answer is C. (B, 3/2, is the first term: a lower bound, not an upper bound.)
